card.band: 4 h. A frontier agent obtains a part of the speedup but not the full-width kernels. A weaker model has no gain. Buckets by quant type and shape class.
card.cheat: Caching results or reducing precision. Inputs are random per run and the output gate is exact within tolerance.
card.grading: The median wall-clock of a kernel bench over a set of shapes. A hard gate requires output equality to the baseline within a tolerance on random tensors. The reward is 2^u-1 against the reference's speedup.
card.reference: Written by us from the known vectorisation pattern, and the speedup is measured at build. The subject is likely close to the existing quantised dot-product task, so it must differ in its shapes and quant types, or be dropped if judged a duplicate.
card.source: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/2212 (lever moved from Metal to x86 CPU), MIT
card.task: /app ships a snapshot of the ggml CPU backend where the Q4_0 and Q4_1 matrix-vector and small-batch matmul kernels are in a slower, scalar-leaning form. The agent speeds them up with AVX2 and AVX-512 where available, using blocking, unpacking and threading, while keeping the same results. The delivery is the buildable tree and the test binary.

v1.kill_reason: The reference is upstream llama.cpp CPU kernel code that is public in git history (commits 1bfc153e, 581c3051) and recallable, so the grading cannot be sealed; the cited source PR #2212 is a Metal change, not x86, so the stated lever is contradicted; K1 risk also applies given neighbour S-op-002 at 0.485.

Band.why: 4 h band asserted with no dated public evidence; at most 3 without it.

Build.why: Smoke build 361 s and suite 281 s; well inside 5 days.

Fit.why: CPU-only and fits 8 cores and 16 GB, but AVX-512 depends on host hardware.

Hor.why: Kernel work is substantial but narrow; 4 h tier is plausible for the scope.

Lic.why: MIT, confirmed at the LICENSE file; shipping allowed.

Multi.why: Quant types times shape classes give several buckets with partial credit.

Nov.why: Close to public quantised dot-product subject (S-op-002 at 0.485, S-op-004 at 0.402); same subject and deliverable family.

Real.why: Repo is real and MIT, but the cited PR is Metal, not x86, so the paper trail for the stated lever is contradicted.

Ref.why: Reference would be ours but is effectively upstream code, so it is strong on paper yet trivially reproducible.

Seal.why: Reference and original kernels are recallable from upstream history and memory, so the answer is not sealable.

Surf.why: Shape and quant buckets give a moderate surface; no executable oracle or unlimited generator is defined.

spike_plan.kill_if: Upstream AVX kernels can be recovered from history or recalled, or the 4 baseline failures cannot be explained as environment.
spike_plan.pass_if: Mutated base is not reversible to upstream within a bounded effort, and the baseline suite is stable with 4 failures excluded.
steps: Read the smoke-build test output to identify the 4 stable baseline failures and decide whether they are environment or real; exclude them from any gate.

In the upstream repo history, locate the ggml-cpu Q4_0 and Q4_1 vec_dot AVX2/AVX-512 implementations at the snapshot's commit and confirm the mutated base differs from them by a bounded set of functions.
Check whether the degraded base can be diffed back to the upstream code, which tells us if git history stripping is enough to seal it.
Measure baseline vs upstream-optimized kernel median times on two shapes to see the achievable speedup ceiling.
Decide: if upstream history is present in the snapshot or the kernels are recallable, kill as K11; if the mutation is large and not recoverable, reconsider with a different sealed subject.

v1.summary: The seed's source PR #2212 is a merged Metal GPU change, not an x86 CPU lever, so its paper trail is contradicted, although the llama.cpp repo itself is real and MIT. Because the optimised Q4_0/Q4_1 AVX kernels already exist in upstream public history and are recallable, the grading cannot be sealed and the task is killed as K11.
